title: Portfolio Website
subtitle: A premium Scandinavian-minimal portfolio built with Tailwind CSS, dynamic photo upload, floating dock navigation, and Formspree contact form — the site you're looking at right now.
overview: Every platform engineer needs a portfolio, but most tech portfolios look the same: dark theme, terminal aesthetic, monospace everything. I wanted something different — a warm, editorial design inspired by Scandinavian minimalism that felt premium without being pretentious.

The portfolio is built with zero build step: pure HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with Tailwind CSS loaded via CDN. Everything is config-driven — change config.json and the entire site updates. It features a floating dock navigation, animated hero entrance, dynamic photo upload with localStorage persistence, and a Formspree-powered contact form.
The result is a site that's fast (no bundler overhead), maintainable (one JSON file controls all content), and visually distinctive enough to stand out in a sea of dark-themed developer portfolios.
challenge: The Problem: Most developer portfolios are either template-based (looking identical to thousands of others) or require a full build pipeline (Next.js, Gatsby) that adds complexity disproportionate to the content. I wanted a portfolio that was uniquely mine, performant, and maintainable without a build step.

The design challenge was balancing editorial aesthetics with developer portfolio conventions. Readers expect to see projects, skills, and contact info — but the presentation needed to feel more like a design magazine than a GitHub profile.

Technical constraints included: no build step (pure CDN-based), mobile-first responsive design, smooth animations without performance degradation, and a photo upload feature that persists without a backend.
solution: I chose Tailwind CSS via CDN for utility-first styling without a build pipeline, combined with custom CSS for glass morphism effects, animations, and the gradient mesh background. The entire design system lives in Tailwind's config and styles.css.

The architecture is config-driven: config.json contains all content (hero text, project descriptions, awards, social links), and script.js reads it on load and renders everything dynamically. This means updating content requires editing one JSON file, not HTML.

For the floating dock, I built a macOS-style glass navigation bar that tracks the current section via IntersectionObserver and highlights the active link. Smooth scrolling and hover-expand animations make it feel native.

Photo upload uses the File API to read images as data URLs and stores them in localStorage. This gives instant preview without a backend, and the photo persists across sessions. A default photo from the repo is shown if no upload exists.

architecture.heading: Config-Driven Rendering
content: The config.json file is the single source of truth for all content. On page load, script.js fetches it, merges with defaults, and calls applyConfig() which renders every section: hero, about, projects, awards, personal projects, contact, social links, audio widget, footer, and dock.

This means the site can be completely re-skinned by editing one JSON file. No HTML editing required. The same pattern applies to the case study pages — each project's content lives in a JSON file under case-studies/data/.

architecture.heading: Animation System
content: The site uses a two-tier animation system: Hero entrance (staggered fade-up on page load with 120ms delays) and scroll reveal (IntersectionObserver triggers fade-up when elements enter viewport). Both use cubic-bezier easing for natural motion.

The hero features decorative animated elements: spinning concentric rings around the profile photo, CSS-animated audio bars in the widget, and a gradient mesh background with radial gradients. All animations are GPU-accelerated (transform + opacity) for 60fps performance.

timeline.title: Design System
timeline.description: Defined color palette (cream/charcoal/terra), typography scale (Inter/Playfair/JetBrains Mono), and component patterns (glass surfaces, tech tags, project cards). Set up Tailwind config.

timeline.title: Layout & Sections
timeline.description: Built the 12-column grid layout, all 7 sections (hero through contact), and the responsive breakpoints. Implemented the floating dock navigation.

timeline.title: Config System
timeline.description: Built the config-driven rendering engine in script.js. Created config.json with all content. Implemented the applyConfig() function for dynamic rendering.

timeline.title: Interactivity
timeline.description: Added hero entrance animations, scroll reveals, photo upload with localStorage, live clock, availability indicator, and contact form with Formspree.

timeline.title: Polish
timeline.description: Fine-tuned animations, added glass morphism effects, gradient mesh background, custom scrollbar, selection styles, and focus states. Responsive testing across devices.

learnings: No build step is a feature, not a limitation. The CDN-based approach means the site deploys as static files to GitHub Pages or Vercel with zero configuration. There's no node_modules to corrupt, no bundler to debug, no dependency updates to manage. For a portfolio site, this is the right tradeoff.

Config-driven architecture scales to case studies. The same pattern (JSON data + template rendering) that powers the main site also powers the case study pages. Adding a new case study is just creating a JSON file — no HTML, no build, no deployment complexity.

Glass morphism needs restraint. The temptation with backdrop-filter is to glass everything. I limited it to the dock, time widget, audio widget, and buttons — surfaces that float above content. Overuse makes the UI feel blurry rather than premium.

Editorial design works for tech portfolios. The Playfair Display headings, generous whitespace, numbered sections, and asymmetric grids give the site a magazine-quality feel that differentiates it from the typical dark-theme developer template.
